tagline.value: Forecasting software that keeps distributed energy grids stable.

sector.value: Energy / grid analytics software (SaaS for electric distribution utilities)

answer.value: Verdant Grid sells forecasting software to US electric distribution utilities. The deck states it ingests smart-meter and inverter telemetry and produces 15-minute-resolution generation forecasts per feeder, delivered as a read-only SaaS layer alongside a utility's existing SCADA system with no utility-side hardware and no control-plane integration. It is raising a seed round in 2026.

The deck implies a why-now through the growth of distributed generation: it cites 8.2 TWh of renewable curtailment in 2025 and says legacy SCADA forecasting tools were built for centralised thermal plants, and it sizes its SAM as the 420 utilities already above 5% distributed generation penetration. However, no explicit 'why now' slide, regulatory trigger, or technology inflection is named, so the timing case is inferred rather than argued.

The deck states that US utilities curtailed 8.2 TWh of renewable generation in 2025 because they cannot forecast distributed solar and battery output hour-by-hour, and that curtailment cost operators an estimated $1.4B last year. No source is given for either figure. The framing is that this loss is attributable to forecasting inability rather than to transmission or market constraints, which the deck asserts without support.

The deck says the incumbent approach is legacy SCADA forecasting tools, which it describes as built for centralised thermal plants rather than distributed resources. It quantifies the incumbent's performance as an 11.7% mean absolute error against Verdant Grid's 4.1%. The budget holder is implicitly the distribution utility, since the four paying customers are utilities, but the deck does not name the incumbent vendors, the internal buyer, or what utilities currently spend on these tools.

The product is an annual SaaS subscription priced per feeder under management. It ingests smart-meter and inverter telemetry and outputs 15-minute-resolution generation forecasts for each feeder, running as a read-only layer beside the utility's existing SCADA. The deck emphasises that this means no utility-side hardware, no control-plane integration and no NERC CIP scope, which it presents as easing deployment. The forecasting method or model architecture is not described.

The only technical evidence offered is a stated mean absolute error of 4.1% versus 11.7% for the incumbent baseline. The deck does not say which incumbent, over what period, on how many feeders or utilities, or whether the comparison was run in production or backtested. Commercial evidence is four paying utility customers, 128% net revenue retention and zero logo churn to date.

Two named executives: Dr. Amara Oyelaran, CEO, with 9 years at PJM Interconnection leading day-ahead forecasting and a PhD in power systems from Georgia Tech; and Ben Kaur, CTO, a former staff engineer on Tesla Autobidder. An unnamed advisor is described as the former Chief Grid Officer of a top-10 US investor-owned utility. The deck does not state whether either founder is full-time, headcount, or equity split.

The deck names no gaps explicitly, but the use of funds implies the main missing capability is utility sales: 45% of the $4M is earmarked for five utility-sales hires, and 20% for SOC 2 Type II and utility security review, suggesting no dedicated compliance or security function today. The only named external relationship is the EPRI distribution working group, which sources the eleven-utility pilot pipeline; the advisor is described by title only and not named.

The deck puts TAM at $750M, derived bottom-up as 3,000 US electric distribution utilities times a $250K average annual contract value, and says the pricing input comes from current contracts. SAM is roughly $105M, being the 420 utilities with more than 5% distributed generation penetration. Note a contradiction: the TAM uses a $250K average contract value while the business model slide states an average contract value of $155K (slides 5 and 6); at $155K the TAM would be about $465M and the SAM about $65M. No SOM is given.

Revenue comes from an annual SaaS subscription priced per feeder under management, with an average contract value of $155K and a land-and-expand motion from one district to a utility's full service territory. The deck states gross margin of 81% and net revenue retention of 128%. It does not disclose CAC, sales cycle length, or payback period.

The deck names no competitor. It refers only to 'legacy SCADA forecasting tools' built for centralised thermal plants and to an unnamed 'incumbent baseline' against which it claims 4.1% versus 11.7% mean absolute error. The differentiation axis is therefore forecast accuracy plus low-friction deployment (no hardware, no control-plane integration, no NERC CIP scope), quantified only on accuracy and against an unidentified comparator.

The deck reports $620K ARR, up from $180K twelve months earlier, and four paying utility customers, two of them on multi-year contracts. It states net revenue retention of 128% and zero logo churn to date, plus an eleven-utility pilot pipeline sourced through the EPRI distribution working group. No grants, non-dilutive funding, or prior financing history are mentioned, and the pipeline utilities are not stated to be contracted or paying.

External validation consists of four paying utility customers, two on multi-year contracts, and an eleven-utility pilot pipeline reached via the EPRI distribution working group. An advisor described as the former Chief Grid Officer of a top-10 US investor-owned utility is cited. No customer, pilot participant, investor, or advisor is named, and the deck says the seed lead is not yet named despite $1.6M committed.

The deck does not include a risk slide and names no risks directly. It gestures at two risk areas through mitigations: deployment and cybersecurity risk, addressed by the read-only architecture with no utility-side hardware, no control-plane integration and no NERC CIP scope; and procurement/security-review risk, addressed by allocating 20% of the raise to SOC 2 Type II and utility security review. Technical, regulatory and financing risks are otherwise unaddressed.

Three specific gaps. First, the market maths contradicts itself: TAM is built on a $250K average annual contract value while the business model slide reports an actual average of $155K (slides 5 and 6), so the stated $750M TAM and $105M SAM are overstated by roughly 60% on the company's own pricing. Second, the growth plan does not reconcile arithmetically: reaching $3M ARR from $620K within 24 months needs about $2.4M of net new ARR, or roughly 15 additional contracts at $155K, against a base of four customers and an eleven-utility pilot pipeline (slides 4, 6, 8). Third, revenue concentration is severe — four customers produce $620K, so a single loss is a material event, and the 128% NRR and zero churn claims rest on that same base of four. The deck also claims 'no NERC CIP scope' while simultaneously budgeting 20% of the raise for utility security review, which suggests security diligence is a real gating item in the sales cycle rather than a solved one.

The deck states a $4M seed raise with $1.6M committed and no lead named yet. It omits the instrument (priced equity, SAFE or note), valuation or cap, discount, interest, maturity, pre- or post-money framing, and the identity of the committed investors. A partner would need all of those before proceeding.

Use of funds is 45% to five utility-sales hires, 35% to forecasting model R&D, and 20% to SOC 2 Type II and utility security review. The deck says the raise buys 24 months of runway to $3M ARR. That milestone requires roughly quadrupling ARR from $620K within the runway window; the deck offers no ramp assumptions, quota per rep, or sales-cycle length for utility buyers to support it.
